Puss in Boots: The Last Wish Review, Cast & Ending Explained

Key Takeaways for Readers

  • Antonio Banderas returns as Puss realizes he has burned through eight of his nine lives.
  • Director Joel Crawford introduces dynamic, painterly anime-style combat sequences.
  • Wagner Moura delivers an instantly iconic vocal performance as the chilling villain Death.
  • The poignant finale rejects the pursuit of immortality in favor of cherishing a single, meaningful life.
🎯 AUDIENCE & WATCHLIST GUIDE
✓ Who Will Love This:

Animation enthusiasts, Shrek franchise fans, and anyone looking for a visually inventive adventure with real emotional weight will love this.

⚠️ Who Should Pass:

Skip this if you are seeking a lightweight, purely slapstick cartoon without darker themes or tense, frightening villain encounters.

A Legendary Hero Confronts His Final Mortality

After centuries of reckless swashbuckling, Puss in Boots faces a harsh reckoning: eight of his nine lives are gone. Shaken to his core by a chilling duel with a hooded, sickle-wielding bounty hunter, Puss retreats to the mundane sanctuary of Mama Luna's cat shelter. His exile is cut short when news emerges of a magical Wishing Star hidden deep within the treacherous Dark Forest. Teaming up with the irrepressibly cheerful therapy dog Perrito and his estranged flame Kitty Softpaws, Puss embarks on a desperate quest to restore his lost lives before fate catches up with him.

Ending Explained: The Truth Behind Death's Sickles

The climactic showdown atop the crumbling Wishing Star crystallizes the film's existential weight. The mysterious bounty hunter drops his disguise, revealing he is not a mere assassin, but literal Death come to claim a feline who brazenly mocked mortality. Instead of wishing for unearned extra lives, Puss chooses to stand his ground and fight to protect his friends. Seeing Puss genuinely value his remaining days, Death lowers his dual sickles and departs with begrudging respect. Puss, Kitty, and Perrito abandon the wishing map, resolve to live their singular lives to the fullest, and set sail toward Far Far Away.

Vocal Mastery and a Daring Visual Pivot

Antonio Banderas infuses his signature character with unprecedented vulnerability, balancing theatrical bravado with raw panic attacks. Wagner Moura steals every frame with a sinister, spine-tingling whistle that became an instant viral sensation across social media. Behind the camera, director Joel Crawford ditched traditional computer-generated hyperrealism for a stylized, hand-drawn aesthetic inspired by Sergio Leone westerns and modern anime classics like Akira. Dropping framerates during combat gave every acrobatic strike an electric, comic-book punch, permanently raising the bar for DreamWorks Animation's visual output.

Critical Verdict: Why This Family Hit Transcends Ages

Rated PG for mild rude humor and intense sequences, the film handles mature themes of mortality and anxiety without patronizing younger viewers. It balances genuine fairy-tale dread with laugh-out-loud physical comedy, anchored by Harvey Guillén's tender voice work as Perrito. Boasting a remarkable 95% critical consensus, this standout adventure outshines its predecessors by trusting its audience to navigate emotional depth alongside blockbuster set pieces. Whether streaming at home or watched on a big screen, it delivers an unforgettable cinematic ride for both parents and seasoned animation buffs alike.

EDITOR'S TAKE

Far more than a simple Shrek spinoff, this vibrant sequel delivers breathtaking action and surprisingly mature heart. It ranks among the finest animated releases of the decade.
